summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are legal throughout Benin. Article 545 of the new Penal Code, in force since 2018, provides an equal age of consent regardless of sex and retains greater penalties only for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex.

Beninese law provides no pathway for legal gender recognition.

Beninese law provides no general prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and no specific protection against discrimination based on gender identity. Same-sex couples and families have no legal recognition.

Narrow protections exist but do not amount to general anti-discrimination coverage. Article 394 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code (2017) and Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law restrict processing of personal data revealing sex life or sexual orientation, Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 (2012) requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist acts based on sex or real or perceived sexuality that infringe the rights and dignity of women or girls, and Article 552 of Law No. 2017-20 punishes provocation of discrimination, hatred or violence based on sexual orientation through an electronic communications network or computer system with one year imprisonment and a five million CFA francs fine, or one of those penalties only, in place since 2018.

Despite legality, the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct.

Healthcare denial is documented as routine. Providers regularly refuse LGBTQ-related treatment including gender-affirming hormone therapy and also deny general care such as malaria treatment, and LGBTQ persons are typically denied medical care and social services. A foreign government country report for 2023 assesses hostility as most pronounced outside major urban areas, a pattern visitors should weigh in movement planning.

Physical safety risk from private actors is severe. Anti-gay lynchings are reported as commonplace, with broader findings of arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment committed mostly by civilians rather than state authorities while police rarely pursue perpetrators. Persons reporting violence or discrimination conceal sexual orientation or gender identity out of fear of mistreatment.

Two findings single out transgender persons within that broader stigmatization. Priests are documented as calling transgender people demons, and hiring discrimination is reported to affect especially transgender and intersex people.

For partners, Benin grants diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. That exception stands apart from the general absence of couple recognition.
tangentialFactors:
A 20-place temporary accommodation centre operated by the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020. Almost 380 young people from Benin and the subregion passed through it between 2020 and 2024, indicating small survivor-support infrastructure alongside the violence risk.

Public assembly by LGBTQ associations has occurred. On 17 May 2013 associations in Cotonou organized a public International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event at the Institut Francais drawing 200 people.

A 31 August 2015 press report commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups recorded LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describing discrimination and persecution from churches and governments. Given its date, it is context on religious-institution hostility rather than current-state evidence.

Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restriction for LGBT people.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register in Benin.

Residents face sustained employment and family exclusion. Employers often will not hire people known to be LGBTQ, and LGBTQ people are frequently rejected by families and have difficulty getting jobs.

Religious pressure is a significant source of harm for residents. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries, Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques participate in homophobic preaching, and imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion therapy often coerced by families. Homosexuality is widely perceived as unnatural and foreign, described as a disease brought by white people and as stemming from Western culture, with homosexuals treated as deviants.

Article 104(d) of the Children’s Code Law 2015-08 bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption.

Legal history confirms that adult consensual conduct was never criminalised under the provisions cited in the sources. Article 331 of the old Penal Code and a 1947 amendment punished only an indecent act or act against nature with a minor of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a 200 to 50,000 francs fine. Article 88 of the 1996 draft Penal Code would have punished an indecent act or act against nature with an individual of the same sex with one to three years imprisonment and a 100,000 to 500,000 francs fine but was never voted into law, and the October 2008 draft contained no punishment for same-sex relations between consenting adults in private and was not voted on. Benin’s representative stated for the 2008 review that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered although provided for by law because families would never allow children to be taken to court. Benin rejected recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons in the 2012 review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting that certain things would be rectified.

For the 2023 Universal Periodic Review the government accepted two of fifteen recommendations, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against HIV. Lesbian, bisexual and queer women rarely report to police.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced provision on bathroom or facilities access for trans persons was found, and that issue remains unresolved for this dossier.

No sourced rule on entry, visa screening or airport screening that risks outing a trans visitor was found, beyond the diplomatic-partner visa exception, and that gap is not sourced.

Sources provide no separate finding on societal tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general LGBTQ stigmatization, beyond the documented priest slur and the hiring finding that singles out transgender and intersex people. Broader trans-specific tolerance remains unresolved.
